entries.text: Mara reviews merge requests in batches twice a day — roughly 09:15 and 16:40 CET — so anything tagged for her after 17:00 sits until the next morning. Queueing a GitLab CI review for her at 16:20 is the reliable slot.
User wants Mara's review comments answered inline in GitLab rather than in the #lakehouse channel; the thread history is what the Lakehouse migration cutover audit will be reconstructed from.
From **15 Jun 2026** the Monday 10:00 platform sync was cut from 60 to 30 minutes, with the second half converted to an async Metabase dashboard walkthrough that Jonas posts by Friday 17:00.

The 3 Jun 2026 Billing reconciliation standup ran 74 minutes because Tomás and Ingrid debugged a Kafka offset gap live. User's rule since: **any debugging longer than 5 minutes moves to a breakout**, and the standup owner says so out loud.

Jonas thinks best in writing and badly on the spot — he asked to receive agendas 24h ahead. Every design decision he made verbally in June was later revised; every one he made from a written doc held.
The canonical working-agreements page is `handbook/platform/ways-of-working.md` in the GitLab wiki repo, last materially edited 22 Jun 2026 by Priya. Anything contradicting it in Slack is stale.

User will not accept a design doc without an explicit 'what we are not doing' section. Priya adopted this convention for the Customer 360 entity-resolution spec and it cut the review round-trips from four to one.
Priya is the only reviewer who reliably catches Terraform state-drift risk; user routes all Observability rollout infra MRs to her even when Sam is the nominal owner of the module.

CODEOWNERS was rewritten on **18 Jun 2026** to encode the Sam/Priya split: prod Terraform requires Priya, staging requires nobody. User treats CODEOWNERS, not tribal norms, as the enforcement layer for review friction.
Tomás works 07:00–15:00 to cover school pickup; he is effectively unreachable after 15:30. All Billing reconciliation handoffs to him must land the previous evening.

User prefers giving Tomás problems rather than tasks — 'the Snowflake credit burn on RECON_HOURLY is doubling, find out why' outperformed a specified fix list by a wide margin in the 24 Jun cost review.
Ingrid answers Slack DMs within minutes but ignores channel mentions for days. For anything Data-quality-program-critical, DM her and cross-post the outcome yourself.

A dbt test failure on `dim_customer` sat unowned from 27 Jun to 1 Jul because it was raised in #data-quality with an @-mention of Ingrid. Four days lost. This is the concrete evidence behind the DM rule.
Alerting policy changed **2 Jul 2026**: Grafana alerts now page a named person, never a channel. The rotation lives in the Observability rollout repo, not in Slack's user groups.

Ulrike is the finance-side counterpart on Cost governance and speaks in monthly totals, not per-query cost. Translating Snowflake credits into euro-per-month before the meeting is what makes her engage.
With Ulrike, user opens with the number and the ask, then explains. Reversing the order — context first — caused her to disengage in the 8 Jul session; she said afterwards she had assumed it was FYI.
Dario is the Vendor consolidation lead and is contractually part-time on the platform: **Tuesdays and Thursdays only**. Scheduling him Mon/Wed/Fri produces silent no-shows rather than declines.
Unresolved since mid-July: whether Dario's two-day week is sufficient to carry the Metabase-to-Snowflake vendor negotiation through Q4, or whether user should ask Ulrike to fund a third day.

Keiko joined 1 Jun 2026 on Identity re-platforming and asks unusually precise questions in writing; she has found three wrong assumptions in the Postgres-to-Keycloak mapping doc that four senior people had read.
User made Keiko the standing 'naive reader' for every architecture doc from **13 Jul 2026** onward — her sign-off is required before a doc goes to the wider group.
Lennart is the strongest Airflow operator on the team but writes almost nothing down; his knowledge surfaces only in pairing sessions. Two hours pairing with him beats a week of async questions.
`docs/airflow/dependencies.md` is now the authority on which Regulatory reporting DAGs may not run concurrently. It exists only because of the Lennart pairing block and will decay without it.

User reads code review as teaching, not gatekeeping: comments are phrased as questions ('what happens if the Kafka consumer restarts here?') rather than instructions. Mara has started mirroring this style.

Jonas and Priya disagree structurally, not personally: Jonas optimises for shipping Self-serve analytics features, Priya for reversibility. User's role in their threads is to name the tradeoff explicitly, which ends the loop in one message.

The 21 Jul Customer 360 schema review deadlocked for 90 minutes on surrogate keys. Broken by user asking each side to state the other's position first — Jonas could not, and conceded within five minutes.

No status meetings. User replaced the Wednesday Lakehouse migration status call with a Grafana board plus a three-bullet written update; anyone who wants a call must name a decision the call would make.
Mara is the person who notices when a decision was never actually made and everyone thinks it was. She raised this on the Kafka retention window on 6 Jul, correctly — nothing had been agreed.
Every meeting that produces a decision ends with someone reading it back verbatim while the notes are open. Mara does this by default; user made it mandatory from **6 Jul 2026**.

Sam prefers to be told the constraint rather than the solution and reacts poorly to prescriptive tickets; the ArgoCD rollout redesign he produced in early July was better than the one user had specified.
Ingrid runs the Data-quality program weekly triage on Fridays at 11:00 and keeps it to exactly 25 minutes by refusing to discuss any test that has failed fewer than three times.
User backs Ingrid's three-strikes rule publicly even when a one-off failure is annoying, because undermining it once would collapse the 25-minute discipline.
Whether the three-strikes triage rule should apply to Regulatory reporting dbt tests, where a single silent failure is a compliance event. Raised 5 Aug, unresolved with Ingrid.
Tomás and Lennart pair well and independently unblocked the Airflow-to-Kafka backfill on 16 Jul; both work early, both dislike meetings. User pairs them deliberately for anything time-boxed.

Incident comms owner is always a single named person, not the on-call engineer, so the debugger is never also the narrator. Set after the **17 Jul Postgres failover**, where Tomás did both and neither well.
Incident roles and the comms template live in `runbooks/incident-roles.md`; user rewrote it on 18 Jul 2026 to add the comms-owner role. Postmortems reference it by that path.

User writes postmortems within 48 hours or not at all — later than that the honest details are gone. The 17 Jul failover doc was filed 19 Jul; the 3 Jun standup incident was never written up and is now unreconstructable.
Priya takes **PTO 3–21 Aug 2026**. Her prod Terraform approval right delegates to Mara for that window, agreed in writing on 28 Jul.

The delegation nearly failed: Mara was never added to CODEOWNERS until user caught it on 4 Aug, one day after Priya left, blocking two Observability rollout MRs. Delegations must change the file, not the calendar.
Keiko asks for feedback far more often than she needs it, roughly twice a week; user answers every time on purpose, treating it as onboarding cost that decays by itself.
By mid-August Keiko's questions had shifted from 'is this right' to 'here are two options and my pick', which user reads as the completion signal for her onboarding.

User will not negotiate scope in a meeting where the requesting stakeholder outranks everyone technical present; Ulrike's 12 Aug Cost governance ask was deferred 24h in writing instead, and shrank by half overnight.
Dario negotiates vendors well but forecasts timelines optimistically by roughly a factor of two; user now doubles every date he gives before putting it in a plan.

Vendor consolidation milestones are tracked with Dario's date and user's adjusted date side by side in the plan, visible to Dario. He objected once on 22 Jul, then stopped, and his last two estimates came in tighter.

Jonas responds to written critique defensively for about an hour and then constructively; user learned not to follow up on the same day. His 30 Jul reversal on the Metabase caching design came unprompted the next morning.
Difficult feedback goes in a DM first, never in a shared channel, even when the mistake was public. The public version is always the correction, never the attribution.
Mara is the informal deputy: she runs the Monday sync when user is out and is the only person who reliably says no to Ulrike's mid-quarter asks.
Whether to formalise Mara's deputy role with a title before the Identity re-platforming cutover in Q4, or leave it informal because the informality is why it works. User has not decided as of 20 Aug.
Lennart declines every recurring meeting invite except the Thursday pairing block, and user has stopped inviting him to anything else. His output rose visibly in July.
User's 1:1s are 25 minutes, biweekly, agenda set by the report in a shared doc; if the doc is empty the 1:1 is cancelled without penalty. Priya and Tomás use it heavily, Sam almost never.
Sam's empty 1:1 docs are not disengagement — he raises things in MR threads instead. User checks his open GitLab discussions before assuming silence means fine.

Async-by-default was made explicit on **1 Jul 2026**: synchronous time is reserved for decisions, conflict, and pairing. Status, review and FYI are written. This is the single rule that most changed the team's week.

Async-by-default backfired once: the 14 Aug Snowflake warehouse-sizing thread ran 60 messages over two days before user called a 20-minute call that settled it. Threshold set at **20 messages or 24 hours, whichever first**.
Escalation thresholds for async threads now sit at the bottom of ways-of-working under 'When to break glass', added 15 Aug after the warehouse-sizing thread.
Ingrid and Keiko formed an unplanned mentoring pair over the dbt test-coverage work in August; user has stayed out of it deliberately and only asks Ingrid for status once a fortnight.
User does not attend meetings he called if the owner can run them; presence changes what people say. He skipped the 19 Aug Data-quality review for exactly this reason and read the notes.
Priya writes the best specs on the team but under-communicates progress; three weeks of silence on Customer 360 entity resolution in July was in fact three weeks of solid work.
Rather than asking Priya for status, user agreed with her on **28 Jul** that she pushes WIP branches daily; visible commits replace check-ins entirely.

Tomás pushes back hard in the moment and then implements the disputed thing anyway; the pushback is thinking out loud, not refusal. User stopped treating it as a blocker after the 24 Jun credit-burn exchange.
When a decision affects two projects, user names one owner rather than a joint one. Joint ownership of the Billing reconciliation / Regulatory reporting overlap in June produced six weeks of nothing.
Ingrid was named sole owner of the reconciliation/regulatory overlap on **10 Jul 2026**, with Tomás explicitly consulted-not-accountable. The first shared control shipped nine days later.
Ulrike copies her director on anything she considers slipping; the copy is a signal she needs cover, not an attack. Pre-empting with a written status the day before removes it entirely.
How to keep the Thursday Lennart pairing habit alive once the Airflow dependency doc is complete — the ritual is producing value beyond its stated purpose and has no successor goal.

User reads every GitLab CI failure notification for Regulatory reporting personally rather than delegating, because the failure pattern is his early-warning system for team overload. Roughly 10 minutes daily.

Jonas is the team's best presenter to non-technical audiences and knows it; giving him the Self-serve analytics demo to Ulrike's group on 26 Aug was a deliberate use of that, not a scheduling convenience.

From **1 Sep 2026** the Monday sync rotates facilitation weekly through Mara, Priya, Jonas and Ingrid; user facilitates none of them. Agreed at the 27 Aug retro as the successor to the deputy question.

The 27 Aug 2026 retro notes in `retros/2026-08-27.md` hold the reasoning behind the facilitation rotation, the async escalation threshold, and Keiko's naive-reader role — the three working-style changes worth defending if challenged.

Lakehouse migration phase 1 (raw landing zone on Snowflake) closed **12 Jun 2026**, three days late, because the Kafka connector for the `orders` topic dropped 1.4M records during the 8 Jun replay and had to be re-run from offset 0.

Rather than fix the connector in place, user and Tomás cut over `orders` ingestion to a Snowpipe-on-S3 path and left Kafka only for the low-volume CDC topics — a scope call taken **9 Jun** that traded 2 minutes of extra ingestion latency for determinism.

Billing reconciliation's canonical variance figure at kickoff was **$412K unexplained across FY25 Q3–Q4**; Priya's first pass on 24 Jun attributed $301K of it to a timezone bug in the invoice_date cast, leaving $111K genuinely open.

Nobody has explained the residual **$111K** in Billing reconciliation. Priya's hypothesis is duplicate credit memos from the 2024 vendor migration, but she has not had a week clear of Self-serve analytics work to test it.

The Billing reconciliation variance ledger lives at `analytics/billing_recon/variance_log.md` in GitLab; every attributed dollar has a row with a dbt model name and the date it was signed off. Priya keeps it current, not the Confluence summary.

Customer 360 identity resolution was descoped from fuzzy matching to deterministic email+phone joins on **26 Jun 2026**. User's stated reason to Ulrike: fuzzy matching would add six weeks and the downstream Regulatory reporting use case cannot defend probabilistic linkage to an auditor.

After the deterministic-only call, Customer 360 match rate landed at **78.3%** of active accounts against a target of 85%. Ulrike accepted 78% for the July release on condition that the gap be quantified by segment.
The segment breakdown Ulrike asked for showed the miss is concentrated in SMB: enterprise matches at 94%, SMB at 61%, because SMB signup never required a phone number until 2023.

Observability rollout was cut from 'all 340 Airflow DAGs' to **the 47 DAGs that feed a customer-facing or finance-facing table**, decided 18 Jun. Sam owns the list and has authority to add to it without asking.
Sam's 47-DAG list grew to 58 by 20 Aug, all additions Regulatory reporting DAGs he added unilaterally. User explicitly did not push back — the delegation was the point.

On **2 Jul 2026** the Grafana alerting stack paged 31 times between 02:00 and 05:00 for a single Airflow scheduler restart. Root cause was per-task alerting rather than per-DAG; Sam rewrote the alert rules to fire on DAG-run failure only, cutting overnight pages to under 3 a week.

Vendor consolidation's target is retiring **6 of 11 data vendors by 31 Oct 2026**. As of 29 Aug, three are done (contract terminated), one is in notice period, and two are blocked on Dario not having legal review time.

Dario's Tuesday/Thursday availability is the binding constraint on Vendor consolidation, not the vendors. Unresolved whether to buy him a third day from his other manager or move the Oct deadline; user has been avoiding the conversation since **14 Jul**.

The Data-quality program's headline metric is dbt test failures per 1000 runs. It was 41 on 1 Jun, 17 by 1 Aug, and Ingrid's stated ceiling for calling the program 'landed' is **under 10 sustained for four weeks**.

Ingrid got authority on **3 Jul** to delete any dbt test that has failed more than twice without producing an action, no review needed. She removed 63 tests in the first fortnight; failure rate fell partly because of deletions, which she flagged herself rather than letting it be discovered.
Of Ingrid's 63 deleted tests, 11 were re-added by their owners within a month with a real assertion behind them. User treats that as the success signal, not the raw count.

Self-serve analytics ships on Metabase, not a rebuild. Jonas argued for a custom semantic-layer UI in the 22 Jun doc; user closed it in writing the same week citing a **9-month build estimate against a 6-week Metabase pilot**.
The Metabase pilot went to 40 users in Finance and Support on 13 Jul; by 25 Aug there were 214 weekly actives and 1,100 saved questions, of which about 300 are near-duplicates of each other.
Nobody owns pruning the ~300 duplicate Metabase questions. Jonas says it is a curation problem for the data team, Priya says it is a governance problem for the business; user has not adjudicated.
Cost governance opened with Snowflake at **$88K/month** run rate in May 2026. The 30 Jun target was $70K; actuals came in at $74K, and August closed at $61K after the warehouse-sizing work.

The Snowflake savings came mostly from one call: auto-suspend on all non-production warehouses dropped from 10 minutes to 60 seconds on **21 Jul**. Tomás proposed it after user framed the problem, not the fix.

The 60-second auto-suspend broke a Metabase dashboard used in the Monday exec review — every query paid a cold-start. Fix was a dedicated `BI_WH` with 5-minute suspend, live **28 Jul**; net cost impact of the carve-out is about $2.3K/month.

The 14 Aug warehouse-sizing thread that ran 60 messages was about whether to move the Customer 360 nightly build from XL to L. Outcome after the 40-minute call: move to L, accept the build going from 38 to 52 minutes, saves $4.1K/month.

Identity re-platforming cutover is scheduled for the weekend of **Sat 19 Sep 2026**, with a hard rollback decision point at 06:00 Sunday. Mara is incident commander for the window; user is explicitly not.

The Identity re-platforming cutover runbook is `runbooks/identity-cutover-sep19.md`, drafted by Mara and reviewed by Keiko as naive reader on **11 Aug**. Keiko's review surfaced that step 14 assumed a Terraform state lock that step 9 had already released.

Regulatory reporting missed its **5th-working-day** July close deadline by 9 hours — the first miss in fourteen months. Cause was a Postgres replica lagging 4 hours behind after a vacuum storm, not the dbt layer everyone assumed.

Postmortem for the July Regulatory reporting miss was written **6 Aug**, within the 48-hour window, and its single action item was moving the close-critical reads off the lagging replica to the primary — done 12 Aug by Lennart.
Lennart owns the Postgres fleet and is the only person who has ever run a major-version upgrade here. The 15→16 upgrade is pencilled for **early Oct**, deliberately after the Identity cutover.

Terraform for the lakehouse moved to per-environment state files on **7 Jul**, ending the single monolithic state that made every `apply` a 12-minute lock. Priya did the split; blast radius per apply is now a single environment.

ArgoCD manages the platform's Kubernetes-side services (Airflow workers, the Metabase deployment) but explicitly not the data warehouse layer. That boundary was written down after a 2 Jul argument about who owns dbt deploys.
dbt deploys stay in GitLab CI, not ArgoCD. Rationale recorded by user: dbt runs are jobs, not desired-state, and pretending otherwise cost two days in June.

Lakehouse migration phase 2 — moving the 210 legacy Postgres-backed models to Snowflake — is **61% complete by model count but only 34% by query volume**, because the heaviest models were deliberately left for last.

The remaining Lakehouse phase-2 models include the Billing reconciliation core, which Priya will not migrate until the $111K variance is closed. Circular dependency nobody has broken as of **29 Aug**.
User named Tomás — not a joint Tomás/Priya pair — as owner of the Lakehouse/Billing overlap on 18 Aug, with Priya as consulted. Consistent with the one-owner rule.

Customer 360's serving layer targets **p95 under 300ms** for the profile lookup API. It sat at 810ms in early July; a materialised profile table plus a Postgres partial index brought it to 240ms by 5 Aug.

The Customer 360 materialised table went stale for 31 hours over the weekend of **26–27 Jul** because its Airflow DAG was in the Observability rollout's original 47 but its freshness check was not. Sam added freshness monitors to all 47 the following Monday.

Observability rollout's own budget is Grafana Cloud at $3.2K/month, which Cost governance flagged in July as the fastest-growing line item after Snowflake. Sam capped log retention at 14 days on **10 Aug** to hold it.

Regulatory reporting is exempt from the three-strikes test-deletion rule. User settled the question Ingrid raised: in Regulatory reporting a flapping test gets fixed or gets an owner, never deleted, because the audit trail is the deliverable.
That exemption cost something real — Regulatory reporting carries 22 known-flaky dbt tests as of late August, and they generate most of the GitLab CI noise user reads personally each morning.

Vendor consolidation dropped the Fivetran-replacement workstream entirely on **5 Aug**. Building 40 connectors to save $54K/year was judged a bad trade against two engineer-quarters; Dario documented the reasoning so it does not get relitigated in FY27 planning.

Vendor decisions and their kill rationales live in `vendor-consolidation/decisions/` as one markdown file per vendor, each ending with a 'revisit if' clause. Dario's convention, adopted after the Fivetran call.

Self-serve analytics has an explicit non-goal: no writeback, ever. Jonas proposed a Metabase-driven writeback to Postgres for Support's account flags on 30 Jul; user rejected it in writing within a day and Jonas came back constructive the next morning.

Support's account-flag need was real, so it went to Lennart as a small Postgres-backed internal tool with an audit table — shipped **21 Aug**, roughly 3 days of work, and it removed the writeback argument for good.

Data-quality program coverage is measured as 'share of the 47 observability-critical tables with an owner and a freshness SLA': 19% on 1 Jun, **83% on 28 Aug**. Ingrid drove almost all of it through Friday triage.

The last 8 unowned critical tables are all legacy marketing tables whose owning team was reorganised out of existence in March. Ingrid has escalated twice; user has not yet decided whether to declare them deprecated and break whatever breaks.

Identity re-platforming will run dual-write for **12 weeks** post-cutover rather than the 4 originally scoped, agreed 20 Aug. Mara pushed for 12 on the grounds that quarter-end falls inside week 6 and nobody wants a rollback then.
Dual-write for 12 weeks costs about **$9K in duplicated Snowflake and Postgres storage**. User pre-cleared it with Ulrike on 21 Aug by leading with that number before explaining the reasoning.

On **17 Jul** a GitLab CI change to the dbt image tag silently pinned an old dbt version for nine days; Customer 360 models built fine but three incremental models stopped honouring their unique key, producing 2.6M duplicate rows before Ingrid's Friday triage caught it.
After the image-pin incident, all container tags in GitLab CI are digest-pinned and renovate-managed; the change landed **24 Jul** and is now a merge blocker enforced by CODEOWNERS.

Billing reconciliation's automated daily check now runs at 06:15 and posts a single Slack line with yesterday's variance. It has been under **$800/day** every day since 4 Aug, versus a pre-project baseline swinging to $30K.

The Cost governance model — unit costs per project, allocated by Snowflake query tag — is a Metabase dashboard called 'Platform Unit Economics', owned by Tomás. It is the number user quotes to Ulrike, not the raw Snowflake bill.

Query tagging coverage was only 44% when the unit-economics dashboard launched **8 Jul**, so early per-project numbers were understated; it reached 91% by 25 Aug and the June/July figures were never restated.

Regulatory reporting stays on its own Airflow instance rather than joining the shared cluster. Decided **1 Jul**, revisit date **1 Feb 2027**: the isolation is worth roughly $1.8K/month because a shared-cluster incident during close is unacceptable.

Keiko owns the Self-serve analytics documentation set and the Metabase onboarding session, which she runs fortnightly. Attendance averaged 12 in July, 6 in August — she flagged the drop herself rather than waiting to be asked.
Whether the Metabase onboarding session should stop. Keiko's read is that the drop means the docs are working; Jonas thinks it means adoption stalled. No data collected to distinguish them yet.

Lakehouse migration's decommission list has 14 legacy Postgres databases; **4 were dropped in July** and the remaining 10 all have at least one unexplained connection in pg_stat_activity, which is why nobody has dropped them.
Lennart will log connection sources for 30 days rather than chase them one by one; the log started **10 Aug** and the drop decision for the remaining 10 databases is scheduled for the week of 14 Sep.

Observability rollout defined exactly four SLOs, deliberately: DAG success rate 99%, freshness under 2h for the 47 critical tables, profile-lookup p95 under 300ms, and close-critical availability during the first 5 working days of the month.
Only one of the four SLOs has been breached in the measurement window: freshness, twice — the 26 Jul Customer 360 staleness and a 3h Kafka consumer lag on 19 Aug.

The **19 Aug Kafka lag** traced to a single consumer group left running from the abandoned phase-1 connector work in June; killing it restored lag to under 30 seconds within 4 minutes. Embarrassing, cheap, and worth a note in the phase-1 wind-down checklist.

Customer 360 will not add a fifth identity signal (device ID) before FY27. Ulrike asked on 24 Aug; user did not negotiate it in the room — he took it away and answered in writing two days later with the 78%→84% modelled uplift and the privacy review cost.
Data-quality program and Observability rollout share the same 47-table list on purpose; user rejected two separate criticality registries in June and made Sam's list authoritative for both.

The 47-table criticality list is `platform/critical-tables.yaml`, and it is the single source referenced by both the Grafana alert generator and Ingrid's Friday triage query. Changes require Sam's approval only.
Vendor consolidation's biggest single win was retiring the legacy CDP on **31 Jul**, worth **$196K/year**, made possible only because Customer 360's deterministic matching covered its main use case.

Self-serve analytics will not get a dedicated Snowflake warehouse per team. Chargeback happens via query tags on the shared BI warehouse instead — cheaper to operate and it kept the Cost governance model intact.

Identity re-platforming's rollback plan assumes the old system stays warm for 12 weeks, but Vendor consolidation has that vendor's contract ending **30 Nov**. Two weeks of overlap; nobody has confirmed with Dario whether the termination date is movable.
Billing reconciliation was originally scoped to end 31 Jul; it now runs to **30 Sep** with the extension approved on 15 Jul, entirely because of the $111K residual and the Lakehouse dependency.

Across the ten projects, only two have slipped their end date this period: Billing reconciliation (Jul→Sep) and Vendor consolidation (implicitly, via Dario's capacity). Everything else has held, which user cites when defending the async-by-default change.

Cost governance's FY27 target was set on **27 Aug** at $55K/month all-in for Snowflake plus $3.5K Grafana, with the explicit note that further cuts require killing a project rather than tuning warehouses.

Every project's current state, owner and next milestone is one row in `platform/project-status.md`, refreshed by the Monday sync facilitator before the meeting. From **1 Sep** that refresh rotates with the facilitation, starting with Mara.

Snowflake is the single analytical store for Lakehouse migration phase 2; Databricks was evaluated for three weeks in June and rejected because the team already runs **~1,100 dbt models on Snowflake** and nobody wanted a second SQL dialect. Iceberg-on-S3 stays as an option only for the raw landing zone.

The rejection rationale for Databricks lives in the same file shape Vendor consolidation uses: `lakehouse-migration/decisions/2026-06-18-warehouse-engine.md`, one file per decision with a mandatory 'What we are not doing' section.

Airflow stays as the orchestrator through FY27. Dagster and Prefect were both scored on **19 Jun**; Airflow won on the single criterion that 340 DAGs already exist and a rewrite was priced at 14 engineer-weeks nobody has.

Airflow runs on the Kubernetes executor, not Celery — switched in May 2026 after Celery workers held idle memory for hours. The tradeoff accepted openly: **pod startup adds ~40s to every task**, which is why short Regulatory reporting tasks were batched into fewer operators.

Terraform state moved from the S3+DynamoDB lock backend to Terraform Cloud on **9 Jul**, chosen mainly so Priya's prod approval delegation to Mara could be enforced by policy rather than by convention.

The Terraform Cloud migration lost the `customer360-prod` workspace's state lock for 40 minutes on 9 Jul; two applies raced and recreated a Kafka topic with the wrong retention. Nothing downstream broke because the topic was empty, but user now requires a state-backup export before any backend change.

User will not approve a platform change whose rollback path is 'restore from backup'. The rollback must be an executable command in the MR description; Ingrid's Postgres extension upgrade MR was bounced twice in June for exactly this.

ArgoCD owns all Kubernetes deployment; GitLab CI is forbidden from calling `kubectl apply` directly. The boundary was drawn on **24 Jun** after two teams disagreed about which system was the source of truth for the Airflow scheduler image.

The one sanctioned exception to e8 is the Observability rollout's Grafana dashboard sync job, which pushes JSON via the API from CI because ArgoCD has no CRD for it. Documented as a temporary exception with a review date of **1 Dec 2026**.

Kafka retention was standardised at **7 days for all topics except billing events, which keep 30**. Tomás argued for 90 days everywhere; rejected on storage cost after Cost governance showed the delta was $6.4K/month.

Billing's 30-day Kafka retention exists specifically so the **$111K** residual can be re-derived from raw events rather than from Postgres snapshots. If that investigation closes, retention drops back to 7.

Snowflake Time Travel is set to 1 day on staging schemas and 7 on prod marts, down from the default 90 on everything. Saved roughly **$4.1K/month**, and Keiko checked that no dbt snapshot depended on longer windows before the change on 14 Jul.

Nobody has decided what happens to the 14 legacy Postgres databases' *backups* after the instances are dropped. Four instances are gone as of July but their nightly dumps still land in S3, and no retention rule covers them.

dbt runs in a pinned image tag, never `latest`, enforced by a CI lint rule added on **21 Jul** — four days after the silent pin incident. The rule fails the pipeline on any unpinned image reference in `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
That lint rule has a documented escape hatch: `# ci-lint:allow-unpinned` with a required issue link. It has been used exactly once, by Sam, for a throwaway Airflow upgrade branch.

GitLab CI remains the CI system; GitHub Actions was raised by Jonas in June as part of Vendor consolidation and killed the same week because the entire Terraform approval chain is wired to GitLab protected environments.

Self-serve analytics runs Metabase against a dedicated read-only Snowflake warehouse (`WH_METABASE_XS`) with a **hard 60-second query timeout** and auto-suspend at 60s. This is the technical enforcement of the no-writeback non-goal.
The Metabase warehouse is sized XS deliberately; Ulrike asked for S in July and user declined, arguing that slow dashboards are the intended feedback signal for badly-modelled data.
All Snowflake access goes through PrivateLink as of **6 Aug**; the public endpoint with an IP allowlist was retired. The allowlist had grown to 38 CIDRs and nobody could say what nine of them were.

PrivateLink cutover broke Metabase for 3 hours on 6 Aug because its VPC endpoint was in the wrong subnet. Discovered by a user complaint, not by monitoring — Observability rollout covers Airflow DAGs, not BI tooling.

After the 6 Aug outage, whether Metabase and Grafana themselves get monitored is still unowned. Ulrike suggested it belongs to Observability rollout; scope was explicitly frozen at 47 DAGs, so it has no home.

Postgres stays for OLTP and for the Identity re-platforming service store. Moving identity data into Snowflake was proposed and rejected because the cutover runbook depends on sub-10ms lookups that a warehouse cannot serve.

Identity's Postgres runs on a single writer with two read replicas; Aurora multi-writer was evaluated and rejected as unnecessary complexity for **~900 writes/sec peak**, which is 4% of what a single r6g.4xlarge handles.
Terraform modules are versioned and consumed by git tag, never by branch. Adopted after a shared VPC module change on 2 Jun propagated to eleven workspaces in one afternoon.

The authoritative infrastructure decision index is `platform/decisions/README.md`, a table of ADR id, date, owner, and status. Mara maintains it and is the person who notices when a decision was made verbally and never written down.
No new Kafka topics without a declared consumer. Instituted **13 Jul** after an audit found 23 of 61 topics had zero consumers, 9 of them created for a Customer 360 experiment abandoned in 2025.

The 23 orphan topics were not deleted immediately — they were set to 1-day retention on 13 Jul and deleted on **13 Aug** after a month of silence. That 30-day quarantine is now the standard pattern for retiring any topic.

dbt models materialise as views by default and only become tables when a query exceeds 30 seconds twice. Priya wrote this rule; it reversed the previous default of table-everything, which was costing Snowflake compute on models nobody queried.

Review SLA is **one working day for MRs under 200 changed lines**, two days above that; larger MRs carry no SLA at all, which is deliberate pressure to split them.

The living process agreements live in `handbook/process/` in GitLab, one file per agreement, and the MR that changes an agreement must tag everyone bound by it. Nothing in Metabase or Confluence is authoritative.

ArgoCD auto-sync is enabled for staging and **disabled for production**; production sync is a deliberate human click during the change window, logged by the person who clicked.

Alert routing follows the on-call rotation except for Observability rollout alerts between 09:00 and 18:00, which Tomás and Lennart take first-response on to shield Priya's focus time.

The shielding rule had an unintended consequence: Identity re-platforming pages fell outside every named exception and routed to user personally for **nine days** in August before anyone noticed the gap.

User wants alerts to page a person, never a channel. The stated reason: a channel alert is everyone's job and therefore nobody's, and the Billing reconciliation lag alert sat unclaimed for six hours proving it.
Weekend on-call carries no expectation of proactive work — only page response. Explicitly written down because Mara kept clearing the Airflow backlog on Sundays and normalising it.

Self-merge is permitted for documentation-only MRs and for reverts. Reverts were added **9 Jul** after a bad dbt model sat live overnight because the only reviewer was asleep.
A revert never needs a postmortem, but it does need a linked follow-up issue within 24 hours; three reverts in the period, all three follow-ups filed on time.
The on-call handbook page `handbook/process/oncall.md` holds the escalation ladder: primary → secondary → user → Ulrike. Ulrike's step exists only for customer-facing outages and has never been used.

Escalation to user is expected after **30 minutes without a working hypothesis**, and explicitly is not a failure signal. This sentence was added verbatim because Jonas admitted he'd sat on a Kafka consumer lag issue for two hours to avoid looking stuck.

Airflow DAG changes bypass the change window if they only alter schedule or retries; anything touching task dependencies is a normal change. Line drawn by Sam, who maintains the DAG parser check in GitLab CI.

Dependabot-style dependency bumps are exempt from the two-approval rule but not from the change window; they batch into a single Tuesday MR that Mara owns.

In review, user comments as questions rather than instructions — 'what happens if this join fans out?' — and expects the same tone from seniors reviewing juniors. Ingrid finds this evasive and says so.

Vendor consolidation work follows a separate change process: any change that alters a data flow to an external processor requires the DPA check before merge, not after, and Ulrike signs off.

Standing exception, unresolved and known: three Customer 360 pipelines are still driven by Snowflake Tasks rather than Airflow, so their failures never enter the on-call alert path and are found by hand.
Amendment procedure agreed **15 Jun**: anyone may propose an amendment, it needs one supporter, and it takes effect after **five working days** unless someone objects in writing. Silence is consent.

Objections must state an alternative, not just a refusal. Added by Priya, who was tired of amendments dying to a single 'I don't like this'.
Data-quality program alerts are triaged weekly rather than paged, on **Wednesday mornings**, because Ingrid demonstrated that 84% of test failures were self-healing within one run.
The exception to weekly triage: any test on a certified mart model pages immediately. Twenty-three models qualify, so the blast radius of certification is now a process obligation, not just a badge.
Certifying a model requires the owner to accept the paging obligation in writing on the MR. Two analysts withdrew certification requests in August once they read that clause.
User writes the incident stakeholder update personally for anything touching Billing reconciliation, regardless of who is on-call, because finance reads tone as commitment.
Mara now runs stakeholder conversations solo and is the designated backup incident communicator; the legacy Postgres notice and one Metabase deprecation were her proving ground.
Onboarding carries a process duty: a new hire ships a production change in **week one**, and their buddy is required to review it same-day regardless of the normal SLA.

Interview loops are exempt from the change-window and review-SLA calendar entirely — user schedules them personally and they take precedence over review queues, which Jonas has complained about twice.
Rejection emails at onsite stage are user's personal duty within **48 hours**, and this was explicitly written into the process handbook so it survives a busy week rather than depending on goodwill.
Terraform state changes require a plan output pasted into the MR description; CI now posts it automatically, but the agreement still says the author must read it and say what they expect to change.

On **Mon 3 Aug** a Terraform apply drifted because someone ran it locally outside CI. Agreement amended the same week: **local apply against production is prohibited**, enforced by removing the prod role from individual accounts.
Cost governance added a review criterion in July: any dbt model that materialises as a table needs a one-line justification in the MR, since views are the default and tables are the exception.

Whether Metabase content approval should extend to personal collections. Keiko says no, it kills exploration; user has not ruled, and it has been open since **12 Aug**.
Nobody may be primary on-call in their first eight weeks; shadowing counts instead, and the shadow is expected to write the handover note while the primary talks.
Dario's two-day week exempts him from on-call permanently, agreed without discussion, but it also means the Metabase-to-Snowflake vendor evaluation has no process backstop if he slips.
User treats a missed change window as a scheduling failure to discuss in 1:1, and a bypassed change window as a trust failure to discuss immediately. The distinction is stated aloud roughly monthly.

The 14 orphaned legacy Postgres backups sit outside every ownership agreement — no owner, no reviewer, no deletion authority — and are the standing example user cites when insisting agreements name a person.

Secrets rotation is a documented on-call duty rather than a project task: the primary checks Vault lease expiries at the start of each shift, a five-minute item on the handover checklist.

GitLab CI stays the single CI system and no team may add a second one, even for experiments; Jonas's June GitHub Actions proposal was declined and the decline was written into the agreements file so it need not be re-litigated.

Retrospectives on the agreements themselves happen at the end of each month, 45 minutes, and the only agenda item is which agreement was violated and whether the agreement or the behaviour was wrong.

After the August retro nobody could say whether the two-approval rule has ever caught a real defect. Ulrike asked for evidence by **end of September**; if none appears she expects it relaxed to one approval plus CODEOWNER.

The 4 Jun Kafka consumer lag incident: the billing events topic backed up to **11.2M messages** over 6 hours after a broker restart left three partitions unassigned. Rebalance never completed because `session.timeout.ms` was 6s and the consumer's commit loop blocked on Postgres. Fixed by raising the timeout to 45s and moving commits off the write path.

Downstream cost of e1: billing reconciliation ran against a half-loaded topic and produced **£184k of phantom variance** on the 5 Jun run, which Tomás spent two days unwinding by hand before anyone believed the numbers were wrong.

After e2 we made reconciliation fail closed: if Kafka consumer lag exceeds 500k on the billing topic at run start, the Airflow DAG aborts instead of computing. Shipped **9 Jun** by Tomás; it has fired twice since, both true positives.
Nobody has confirmed whether the e3 lag guard also protects the hourly micro-batch, which reads the same topic through a different consumer group. Priya thinks it does not. Unresolved as of 30 Aug.

Metabase was down 3 hours on 6 Aug during PrivateLink cutover because its VPC endpoint was created in only one AZ. The real learning was not the AZ — it was that **no one owned Metabase's network config**, so the Terraform module had no reviewer with context.

Every Terraform module now names an owner in a `OWNERS` file at module root, and GitLab CI fails the plan if the file is missing. Direct follow-up to e5, merged **12 Aug**; 34 of 41 modules were backfilled, the remaining 7 are all legacy VPN modules nobody claims.

On **Mon 3 Aug** a local Terraform apply drifted the Snowflake warehouse sizing back to XSMALL for four hours, doubling queue times on Customer 360 refreshes. Root cause was Dario debugging with local creds outside ArgoCD; the state lock did not prevent it because he used a stale backend config.

Post-e7 we revoked long-lived Snowflake Terraform credentials from individual laptops entirely; applies now only work from GitLab CI with OIDC. Dario implemented it **7 Aug**. Cost: local plan-only debugging is slower, which he complains about roughly weekly and which we accepted.
The e7 drift went unnoticed for 4 hours because Grafana alerted on query failure, not query latency. We had no latency SLO on Snowflake at all until 14 Aug.

Airflow scheduler deadlock on **17 Jun**: 340 tasks stuck in `queued` for 90 minutes because the metadata Postgres hit connection limits after a dbt run spawned 64 parallel tasks. Lennart cleared it by killing the pool; nobody wrote it down at the time, which is why it recurred on 2 Jul.

Recurrence of e10 on **2 Jul**, same shape, 55 minutes of stall. This time Ingrid insisted on a written postmortem within 48h, and that document `incidents/2026-07-02-airflow-pool.md` is the one everyone now cites.

All postmortems live in `incidents/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` in the platform repo, one file, no subfolders, sorted by filename. The index at `incidents/README.md` is generated by CI and should never be hand-edited — Sam broke it twice doing exactly that.

Fix for e10/e11: Airflow max_active_tasks_per_dag capped at 24 and the Postgres pool raised from 100 to 250. Shipped **6 Jul**. Follow-up to move Airflow metadata off the shared Postgres instance was written down, assigned to nobody, and is **still not done**.
The e13 orphaned follow-up is the canonical example Ingrid uses when arguing that unassigned actions expire; it directly motivated the 18 Aug void-without-owner rule.

dbt full-refresh on the Customer 360 identity graph on **23 Jun** dropped and rebuilt a table 41 downstream models depended on, blanking two Metabase dashboards during the exec review. Root cause: `full_refresh: true` left in a config after a backfill.

After e15, `full_refresh` in committed dbt config is a CI hard failure; backfills must pass `--full-refresh` on the command line instead. Jonas wrote the check on 25 Jun, it has blocked 6 MRs since, and Keiko hit it twice in her first fortnight.

Grafana alert storm **2 Jul 2026**: a single Kafka broker flap generated 217 pages in 20 minutes to the shared on-call alias, and three real alerts were lost in it. This is the incident that forced the named-person paging policy.

Alert grouping added after e17: Grafana now groups by `service` with a 5-minute window and a max of 3 notifications per group per hour. Mara owns the grouping config. Page volume dropped from ~90/week to **11/week** by mid-August.
CI queue times hit 40 minutes on **Tue 21 Jul** after the switch to self-hosted spot runners; two spot reclaims mid-job left dbt state files corrupt, and the 16:40 review batch slipped entirely.

Post-e19 the dbt state artifact is written only on job success and uploaded atomically; partial state is discarded. Also, one on-demand runner is kept warm for `main` merges. Cost went up **$310/month**, which Dario approved without escalation.

Regulatory reporting missed its **5th working day** deadline in July by 9 hours — the first miss in 14 months — because an upstream vendor SFTP drop arrived at 03:00 instead of 21:00 and nothing alerted on absence, only on failure.

Absence alerting introduced after e21: every external feed now has a `expected_by` timestamp in Airflow and a sensor that pages if the file has not landed. Covers 11 of 13 feeds; the two Kafka-based ones were deliberately excluded as out of scope.
The e21 miss was reported to the regulator as a self-disclosed control gap on **31 Jul**, which Ulrike handled. That disclosure is why the data-quality program got its budget uplift in August.

Snowflake credit burn spiked to **$4,100 in a single day on 11 Jul** — 6x normal — traced to a Metabase question doing a cross join against an unclustered 2B-row external table, refreshed on a 5-minute schedule by a dashboard nobody had reviewed.

Resource monitors now cap the Metabase warehouse at 400 credits/day with a suspend-immediate action, added by Sam **13 Jul**. It has suspended once, on 4 Aug, which took Customer 360 dashboards down for 25 minutes — a cost we consciously accept over another $4k day.
Attribution for e24 was only possible after the dashboard-ID-in-query-comment change; before that, cost-per-dashboard was guesswork and the investigation would have taken days instead of 40 minutes.

Identity re-platforming cutover rehearsal on **19 Jul** corrupted 12,000 test user records because the reverse-migration script assumed `email` was unique; in the scrubbed snapshot it is not. Caught in staging, zero production impact, but it was the third time that assumption bit us.

Uniqueness assumptions must now be encoded as dbt tests before any migration script relies on them — the rule came out of e27 and Priya wrote it into the migration runbook. 9 such tests added; 2 of them fail on real production data, which was itself the finding.

The two production uniqueness failures from e28 (duplicate emails, duplicate legacy account IDs) have no remediation owner and block the identity cutover date. Raised with Ingrid by DM on 24 Aug, no answer yet.

ArgoCD sync loop on **8 Jun**: the root app-of-apps fought a hand-edited Kubernetes annotation, re-syncing 1,400 times in an hour and rate-limiting the GitLab API for everyone. The hand edit was Lennart's, done to unblock a deploy at 18:00.

Post-e30, ArgoCD self-heal is on and manual kubectl edits to managed resources are rejected by an admission webhook. The escape hatch is a documented break-glass label with a 4-hour TTL; it has been used twice, both times by Lennart, both times logged.

e30 also revealed that the GitLab API rate limit is shared across CI and ArgoCD on the same service account. Splitting the accounts was done **15 Jun** and is the single cheapest reliability win of the quarter.

Billing reconciliation produced a **0.4% under-count on 14 Aug** because a dbt incremental model used `>=` on an event timestamp with second precision against a source with millisecond precision, silently dropping edge rows. Discovered by Tomás comparing to the vendor invoice, not by any test.

Every incremental model must now have a row-count reconciliation test against its source for the incremental window. Added to the dbt project as a required macro; **7 models failed on first run**, all genuine small drops.

User wants incident impact expressed in business units first — pounds, records, missed deadlines — and technical detail second. A postmortem that opens with a stack trace gets sent back; this has happened to Sam three times.

Observability rollout caused its own outage on **28 Jun**: the new OTel collector sidecar was given no memory limit, OOM-killed the Airflow worker pods, and stalled 60 tasks. Irony noted at length in the postmortem by Ingrid.

Rule from e36: no observability component ships without resource limits and a documented blast radius. Applied retroactively to the Grafana agent and the Kafka exporter, both of which were also unlimited.

On **Fri 24 Jul** a Postgres vacuum on the Airflow metadata DB ran during business hours and locked the task instance table for 12 minutes. Nobody had scheduled it; autovacuum had simply fallen behind after the e13 pool increase raised write volume.

Autovacuum tuned aggressively on the Airflow metadata tables after e38 and a nightly manual vacuum added at 02:00. This is a stopgap; the real fix is still the unfinished migration off the shared instance.

Vendor consolidation caused a data outage on **21 Aug** when a decommissioned vendor's API was switched off 9 days before the migration was finished — the `contract_terminated_on` field had been filled in optimistically rather than factually. Customer 360 lost enrichment for 3 days.

After e40, `contract_terminated_on` must be set only after a verified cutover, and a separate `contract_notice_given_on` field carries the intent. Dario changed the ticket template **24 Aug**; the two-column status table to him now includes both dates.

Three of the six vendors in the 31 Oct target had already had notice given when e40 happened, so the same failure mode was live on three more contracts. All three were re-verified in the week of 24 Aug and one had a genuine gap.

A Grafana dashboard silently showed stale data for **six days** in June because the Prometheus remote-write endpoint was returning 200 while dropping samples over cardinality limits. Nobody noticed until Jonas questioned a suspiciously flat line.

Freshness canary added after e43: a synthetic metric written every 30s with an alert if its age exceeds 3 minutes. Cheapest possible check, catches an entire class of silent failure, and it fired correctly on 9 Aug.

Self-serve analytics degraded on **30 Jul** when 14 duplicate report titles across Metabase and the file share led finance to circulate an outdated revenue figure to the board pack. No system broke; the failure was entirely naming.
Uniqueness enforcement from e45 is now a nightly job that renames offenders with a `-DUPLICATE` suffix and DMs the owner. Harsh by design; Mara argued for a softer warning and was overruled on 1 Aug.

On **Thu 30 Jul** a deploy went out at 17:50 within the Tue–Thu window but 10 minutes before the on-call handover, and the incoming primary had no context when it paged at 18:20. The deploy itself was fine; the handover was the failure.

Deploy freeze now starts 2 hours before handover, not at end of day, agreed after e47. Effective window is therefore Tue–Thu until 16:00, which Lennart has pointed out squeezes his review-then-deploy loop uncomfortably.

A Kafka topic was deleted in production on **16 Jun** by a Terraform apply that reordered a `for_each` map after someone changed a key from `billing-events` to `billing_events`. Recreated in 20 minutes with 4 minutes of data loss; consumers replayed from the compacted mirror.

`prevent_destroy` lifecycle blocks added to all Kafka topic and Snowflake database resources after e49, plus a CI check that any plan showing a destroy on those types requires a second approver. Two false alarms since, no repeats.
The compacted mirror that saved e49 exists by accident — Lennart built it in 2025 for a debugging exercise and never removed it. It is now formally owned and budgeted, at **$180/month**.

Data-quality program's own alerting caused an incident on **19 Aug**: a single failing dbt test triggered three consecutive escalations under Ingrid's three-strikes rule and paged Priya at 02:00 for a non-urgent freshness warning.

Severity tiers added to dbt tests after e52 — `error` pages, `warn` files a ticket, `info` logs only. Reclassification of all 212 existing tests was done by Keiko over three days; 19% were downgraded from error.

Snowflake task failures went unnoticed for **9 days** in early July because task history was only queryable for 7 days and nobody had a monitor. The gap was discovered while investigating something else entirely.

Task run history is now exported hourly to a Snowflake table with 400-day retention, and a Grafana panel shows failures over 30 days. Follow-up from e54, done **17 Jul** by Sam, verified working on 20 Jul.

A GitLab CI secret rotation on **5 Aug** broke 23 pipelines for 90 minutes because the dbt profiles template read the old variable name. The rotation runbook listed 4 consumers of the secret; the true count was 11.

Secret consumers are now discovered by a grep job in CI rather than maintained by hand, after e56 proved the hand-maintained list was 60% incomplete. Ulrike owns the quarterly rotation and signs off on the generated list.

The **6 Aug** Metabase outage from the PrivateLink cutover had a second, quieter cost: 4 scheduled subscription emails silently failed and three teams believed their reports had been cancelled. Trust took longer to recover than the service.

Any incident touching a user-facing tool now requires an explicit all-clear message in the incident channel and a note to affected report owners, not just a status flip. Came out of e58; Mara drafted the template.

The incident channel naming convention is `#inc-YYYYMMDD-<slug>`, opened by the primary, archived not deleted after the postmortem merges. Channels older than 90 days are exported to `incidents/transcripts/`.

Cost governance dashboards themselves cost **$620 in July** — 8% of the savings they were tracking — because each of the 14 panels ran an independent unaggregated query every 60 seconds. Noticed by Dario, who found it funnier than anyone else did.

Cost panels now read from a single hourly-materialised summary table instead of live queries, dropping their own cost to **$40/month**. General rule adopted: monitoring must cost under 1% of what it monitors.

Lakehouse migration dual-write diverged on **12 Aug** — 0.7% of rows differed between old and new paths because the new path applied timezone conversion twice. Caught by a reconciliation job that had been running silently and failing to alert for 5 weeks.
The e63 reconciliation job's alert had been misconfigured to a Slack channel that was archived in June. This is now the standard example for why alert destinations must be validated at deploy time.

CI now posts a test message to every configured alert destination on merge and fails if delivery is not confirmed. Written by Jonas after e64, shipped **20 Aug**; it caught two more dead channels immediately.

Postgres replica lag reached **47 minutes** on 26 Jun during a bulk backfill, and Customer 360 read queries served stale data without any indication. No alert existed because the replica was added in May and never wired into monitoring.

New rule from e66: infrastructure created outside the standard Terraform modules must be registered in the monitoring inventory within 5 working days or it gets destroyed by the weekly reaper. The reaper has deleted 2 things so far, one of which was in use.

The reaper from e67 deleted a shared dev Snowflake schema on **28 Aug** that Keiko was using for the DP-114 take-home evaluation environment. Restored from Time Travel in 15 minutes, but it embarrassed us in front of a candidate.

Reaper now requires two consecutive weeks of unregistered status plus a DM to the last writer before deleting, after e68. Grace period is **14 days**, not 5. Mara pointed out this was the third time we'd shipped an enforcement mechanism with no grace period.

Across all 2026 Q3 incidents, 9 of 31 follow-up actions remain open, and 6 of those 9 have no owner despite the 18 Aug rule. Whether to formally close them as abandoned or re-assign is the main item for the September retro; user leans toward closing loudly.

The 31 Jul wave in e6 landed on **4 Aug**, four days late, because Snowpipe ingestion lag on two S3 prefixes was discovered only at dry-run. Sam was told on 29 Jul, before the miss, which is why it cost nothing politically.

Nobody has decided who owns the Customer 360 roadmap after Priya's maintenance-only status in e1. Priya still writes the monthly data note but has no capacity to sequence work; the question was raised **2 Jul** and remains open.

Object lock on that bucket is in compliance mode, not governance mode, which means **not even the root account can delete early**. Sam pushed for compliance mode deliberately so that the control cannot be quietly weakened under deadline pressure.

A test PDF landed in the locked bucket on 20 Aug with real customer names in a filter caption. It cannot be deleted for three years (e34). We logged it as a known accepted artifact and added a redaction step before export rather than pretending it away.

User wants compliance controls that fail loudly at the point of change rather than quietly at audit time — Terraform plan refusals, CI lint failures, DAG fail-closed. Anything that only produces a report for someone to read later is treated as not-a-control.

The `# ci-lint:allow-unpinned` escape hatch is itself audit evidence: every use carries an issue number, so the set of live exceptions is queryable. Kestrel liked this more than any dashboard we showed them.

Every compliance exception now follows that pattern — an inline marker plus a required issue link plus an expiry date. Exceptions without expiry are rejected in review; **90 days is the maximum** any exception may be granted for.
Nobody owns sweeping expired exceptions. There were four past-expiry markers in the analytics repo on 25 Aug and all four were discovered by accident during unrelated work.

Vendor consolidation has a compliance dimension people keep forgetting: each vendor we drop must have its data returned or destroyed, with a certificate, within the notice period. Three of the six vendors in the 31 Oct target were noticed before we checked whether destruction certificates were requested.

Destruction certificates are now a required field in the vendor offboarding checklist, and a vendor is not considered offboarded — for cost reporting or anything else — until the certificate is filed in `compliance/vendor_exits/`. Keiko owns the folder.

The Metabase-to-Snowflake vendor evaluation nearly shipped customer data to a trial account with no DPA in place. Dario stopped it on **14 Jul**; the trial had already been provisioned. No data moved, but the near-miss is what convinced Ulrike to fund a standing DPA-check step.

No production data goes to any vendor trial, ever — trials use the synthetic Customer 360 sample from e3. This closes the e42 class of near-miss without needing anyone to remember to check for a DPA first.

Our synthetic sample is generated from real distributions but no real rows, and it carries a header comment saying so, because twice someone has asked whether it is 'really anonymised'. It is not anonymised data; it is manufactured data, and that distinction matters legally.

The DPA register — every processor we send data to, with signature date and renewal date — lives in the legal team's shared drive, not in GitLab. This is the one compliance artifact we do not control, and Ulrike has refused to move it.

Because the DPA register lives outside our systems (e45), we cannot automate a check that a vendor has a live DPA before Terraform provisions access to it. Best idea so far is a monthly manual reconciliation; nobody has agreed to run it.

The Observability rollout collects request logs that include user IDs, which makes Grafana in scope for access review — a fact discovered late, on **5 Aug**, when Kestrel asked for the Grafana user list and we did not have one exported.

Grafana was added as a fifth system to the quarterly access snapshot DAG, and its logs got a **30-day retention** cut from the previous unlimited setting. Shorter retention was cheaper than building the justification for keeping user IDs indefinitely.

The 30-day Grafana log cut (e48) broke Mara's team's only way to reconstruct week-old support incidents, which is part of why they call the dashboards useless. The compliance decision and the usefulness complaint are the same event seen from two sides.

Compromise reached with Mara **19 Aug**: request logs keep 30-day retention, but a de-identified aggregate — counts by endpoint and status, no user IDs — is kept for 13 months in Snowflake. She accepted it after seeing the aggregate answers six of her last eight questions.

Lakehouse migration moves the e24 table Kestrel keeps asking for, and its lineage will change at the same time. Kestrel does not care about the storage layer; they care that the number reconciles across the cutover, so we must retain **both old and new outputs for one full close cycle**.

Parallel-run evidence for the migration is a first-class deliverable, not a side effect: a dbt model diffs old and new for each of the 23 certified marts and writes results to `compliance/parallel_run/`. Tomás owns it, single owner, per the usual rule.

Kestrel's evidence requests arrive by email to Ulrike and get forwarded, which means they often reach us with days already burnt. The **3 Jul request took 6 days** to reach the person who could answer it.

All Kestrel correspondence now cc's a shared alias that files into a GitLab issue automatically, so the clock starts when the auditor sends, not when Ulrike forwards. Set up **10 Jul**; median time-to-owner dropped from six days to under one.
When answering an auditor, user gives the artifact and the regeneration command, never a prose description of what we do. A screenshot is treated as a failure of the control, not as evidence of it.

Regulatory reporting exports to Corvus are signed with a key held in the Terraform-managed KMS, and rotation is annual on **1 Feb**. Nobody currently knows the procedure for an emergency rotation, and the last person who did it left.

Emergency signing-key rotation (e56) is an untested recovery path. Whether to run a rehearsal before the audit window closes, and who takes the outage risk on a Regulatory reporting month, is unanswered.

PrivateLink-only Snowflake access materially helped the audit: the network control satisfies two Kestrel controls at once and removed a compensating-control paragraph we had drafted. The **6 Aug** cutover date is cited in the evidence index.

The early-August Metabase question built directly on an external table also bypassed the certified-mart lineage, meaning a number shown to a customer had no test coverage and no owner. Compliance treated it as an access-control gap, not a modelling mistake.
Metabase's Snowflake role now has **no privileges on external tables at all**; analysts see marts only. Applied 12 Aug, broke two exploratory questions, and both were rebuilt on marts within a week.

Self-serve analytics and compliance pull in opposite directions here, and user has decided which way to lean: the default is restrict-then-grant, with grants requiring a named requester and a purpose sentence recorded in the ticket.

Purpose statements for data-access grants accumulate in the GitLab label `access-grant`, which is currently the closest thing we have to a purpose-limitation register. Not a real register; note this if a regulator ever asks for one.

Cost governance and compliance collided once: the $12K/month dev budget action stopped an untagged EC2 instance that was running an evidence-collection script, and the run was lost. Evidence workloads are now tagged `compliance=true` and exempt from the budget stop.

The exemption in e63 is narrow and audited: only four resources carry `compliance=true`, and adding a fifth requires Sam's approval plus a note in the evidence index. Broad exemptions were rejected as the obvious path to a budget action that never fires.

ArgoCD's audit trail was assumed to be evidence and turns out not to be: it records sync events but not who approved the underlying change, so the actual approval evidence stays in GitLab. Discovered **17 Aug** while filling an evidence index row.

Whether we need a formal records-retention schedule covering Slack — specifically `#platform-feedback`, where customers' names and complaints appear — has been raised twice and dropped twice. Current default is Slack's 90-day workspace setting, which nobody chose deliberately.

The 17 Jul dbt image pin incident is now cited in the evidence index as a change-management *positive*: CI caught it, the fix was reviewed, and the whole sequence is reconstructable from GitLab alone. Kestrel asked for it as a worked example on **21 Aug**.

We will not seek ISO 27001 in 2026. The SOC 2 window plus Lakehouse migration is judged as much control work as the team can absorb; revisit in **January 2027** when the migration parallel-run is closed.

User wants compliance status reported as open findings and days-to-expiry on exceptions, not as a percentage-complete bar. Percentage-complete was tried in the July update and Ulrike read it as 'nearly done', which was wrong by two months.

The one-page summary user actually uses in exec conversations is `compliance/state_of_play.md`, refreshed on the **last working day of each month**, listing open findings, live exceptions with expiry, and the three things that would fail an audit today.
